When a sentence opens with a describing phrase and a comma, the word right after the comma must be the one doing it.
Think of the opening phrase as a name tag. It has to be pinned on the word right after the comma.
Here's the method. When the four choices start with different words, ask: who is doing the opening action? That word goes right after the comma.
Studying the night sky, Maria Mitchell spotted a new comet. Who was studying the sky? Maria Mitchell. She comes right after the comma.
Trap alert. Studying the night sky, a new comet was spotted. Now the comet is studying the sky. That's a dangling modifier.
It works for any opening. Built in eighteen eighty four, the Washington Monument was once the tallest structure. The monument was built, so it goes first.
To test the theory, the researchers built a model. A model can't test a theory by itself. The researchers do the testing.
Watch for the apostrophe s trap. Hiking through the Andes, the botanist's notebook filled up? With apostrophe s, the notebook becomes the who. Notebooks don't hike.
Let's try an SAT style question. After pleading for years, blank. The activists staged a sit in, or pressure on lawmakers increased?
Who was pleading? The activists. So the answer is: the activists staged a sit in protest.
Trap alert. Pressure can't plead. If the word after the comma can't do the opening action, cross it out.
Your turn. Pause the video. As a young writer, blank. Eudora Welty worked as a photographer, or a government agency hired Eudora Welty?
Eudora Welty worked as a photographer. She was the young writer, not the agency.
Remember three things. Find who does the opening action. That word goes right after the comma. And watch out for the apostrophe s trap. Great work.
